paragraphs.heading: Which way the wave shakes
paragraphs.text: Polarization is a property of transverse waves that describes the direction in which they oscillate. In a transverse wave, the oscillation is perpendicular to the direction the wave travels. A taut string, such as a guitar string, is a good example. Depending on how it is plucked, it can vibrate up and down, side to side, or in any direction in between.

paragraphs.heading: Waves that cannot be polarized
paragraphs.text: Longitudinal waves are different. In sound waves in a liquid or gas, the particles always move along the direction the wave is going, so these waves show no polarization. Transverse waves that do show it include light, radio waves, gravitational waves, and shear waves, which are transverse sound waves in solids.

paragraphs.heading: The fields inside light
paragraphs.text: A light wave is made of an electric field and a magnetic field that oscillate together and are always perpendicular to each other. By convention, the polarization direction is the direction of the electric field. In linear polarization, each field oscillates in a single direction. In circular or elliptical polarization, the fields rotate at a steady rate around the beam's direction of travel. The rotation can be right-handed or left-handed.

paragraphs.heading: Making polarized light
paragraphs.text: Light from the sun, from flames and from incandescent lamps is made of short wave trains with an equal mix of polarizations; this is called unpolarized light. A polarizer lets through waves of only one polarization, so passing unpolarized light through it gives polarized light. The most common optical materials leave polarization alone. Materials that show birefringence, dichroism or optical activity, though, treat light differently depending on its polarization, and some are used to make polarizing filters. Light also becomes partly polarized when it reflects off a surface at an angle.

paragraphs.heading: The photon picture
paragraphs.text: Quantum mechanics also lets us treat light as a stream of particles called photons. Seen this way, polarization is set by a property of photons called spin. A photon spins either right-handed or left-handed about its direction of travel. Circularly polarized waves are made of photons with just one kind of spin. Linearly polarized waves are made of photons in a superposition of the right and left states, with equal amplitudes and phases lined up so the wave oscillates in a plane.

paragraphs.heading: Where it matters
paragraphs.text: Polarization is an important quantity in sciences dealing with transverse waves, for example optics, seismology, radio and microwaves. Technologies that depend on it especially include lasers, radar, and wireless and optical fiber telecommunications. Most light sources are incoherent and unpolarized, or only partly polarized. That is because they give out a random mixture of waves with different frequencies, phases and polarization states.
